changes.after: An Arc lets more than one owner keep the same value alive, even across threads.

before:
Arc<T> uses atomic reference counting for shared ownership. Arc can be sent and shared only when its inner type satisfies the required Send and Sync bounds. Arc alone does not make arbitrary inner mutation thread-safe; a Mutex or atomic payload may still be necessary.

Arc::clone(&value) receives a borrowed Arc and returns another strong owner of the same allocation. It does not copy the inner integer into a separate allocation.

Arc::get_mut returns an optional mutable reference only when there are no other Arc or Weak pointers to that allocation. With two strong owners it returns None. After dropping the other owner, this example has unique ownership and receives Some. No threads are started yet; the next lessons separate mutation and thread lifetime.

is_some() takes the returned Option as receiver and reports whether it is Some. It does not extract the mutable reference or change the stored integer.

Expected output or behavior: false
true. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain why Arc<RefCell<T>> does not automatically become a safe shared mutable value across threads. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: An Arc lets more than one owner keep the same value alive, even across threads.
Here `get_mut` asks for permission to change the value directly. With the clone still present, that request fails.
The output is `false`, then `true`. Dropping the clone leaves just one owner, so the second request succeeds.

before.question: If other is a separate Arc::new(7) rather than a clone, what is printed?
choices: false then false because Arc never permits unique access.
false then true because equal integers share an allocation
before.explanation: The independent allocation adds no owner of value, so value remains uniquely owned at both observations.

after.question: If other is a separate Arc::new(7) rather than a clone, what is printed?
choices: false then false because Arc never permits unique access.
false then true because equal integers share an allocation
after.explanation: A separate Arc does not share the first value. Both requests find just one owner.
